Title: [lsj] about deals, unsportsmanlike conduct and play to win

Messages.Author: Fabio "Sooner"
Messages.Body:
Hi all, hi LSJ.

I know these subjects have been debated over here a number of times,
I'd just like to clarify some situations in my head.
I also know that I could just google, but since I have a bunch of
situations to ask about and I just want to make sure if some general
interpretations apply, I fear I'll get distracted by circunstances
mentioned in each thread I find.

Here's the scoop. We've been debating about breaking deals, which
playgroups usually honor deals and what they do with potential
dealbreakers etc. I assumed all involved were talking about casual
play since there's no rule enforcing deals. At some point, someone
said that players in his playgroup do not accept to play (casual) with
dealbrakers and will gang up on any known dealbreaker during
tournaments - he's got to be the first to fall in each table if they
can manage it.

For all I remember about the subject, I believe this is prone to
penalties for unsportsmanlike conduct, maybe for ignoring the play to
win rule.
In the debate that ensued, some other situations were brought about,
like these (assume sanctioned tournaments for all examples):

- a player who attacks another cross-table because he's the most
accomplished/experient and therefore the "biggest threat" in his path
to the GW;

- a player attacks another cross-table because he's a known
dealbreaker and therefore unlikely for the first to get a good deal
and profit from it to gain the GW later;

- a player attacks another cross-table because he's got the biggest
collection of cards and is likely to have the best deck in the table
(not because of the raw number but because he has the means whatever
he wants, including some proven and tested tournament winner
archetypical decks)

- a player attacks someone cross-table because he does not like [clan
X]

- a player attacks another cross-table because the second has Sudenned
some master of the first that would get in his way later (say, Ventrue
Headquarters)

Does these situations fall on the general concept of unsportmanslike
conduct? I mean, on the "etc." part of:

5.2. Unsportsmanlike Conduct

Unsportsmanlike conduct is unacceptable and will not be tolerated at
any time. Players who engage in unsportsmanlike conduct will be
subject to the appropriate provisions of the V:EKN Penalty Guidelines
and will be subject to further V:EKN review. Judges, players,
spectators, and officials must behave in a polite, respectable, and
sportsmanlike manner. In addition, players must not use profanity,
argue, act belligerently toward tournament officials or one another,
or harass spectators, tournament officials, or opponents. Players must
not play toward goals that conflict with the goal of the game as
stated in the V:TES rulebook (e.g., attacking certain players on the
basis of their V:EKN ratings or overall tournament standing, etc.).

If so, which penalties could be applied? I've been searching for the
V:EKN penalty guidelines mentioned on the tournament rules and just
can't find it.

best,

Thirty seconds' worth of opinion:

Fabio "Sooner" wrote:
|

| win rule.
| In the debate that ensued, some other situations were brought about,

I'll also assume each player is foolish enough to state his motives out
loud, instead of fabricating something random that falls under the "play
to win" rule.

| - a player who attacks another cross-table because he's the most

| accomplished/experient and therefore the "biggest threat" in his path
| to the GW;

I'd bar the action if he actually _SAID_ as much.

However, usually the most accomplished players are also in a good
position game-state-wise, so it's not hard to make the jump from "Must
Kill Goudie" to "Goudie's position is too good, I have to rein him in"
- -- and the second is very hard to rule against because you can't
legislate against stupid play, only illegal play.

| - a player attacks another cross-table because he's a known
| dealbreaker and therefore unlikely for the first to get a good deal
| and profit from it to gain the GW later;

Penalty on the spot. Play to win the current game, not to vindicate
your own personal moral compass. Of course, having that particular
moral compass tends to indicate that you're not sure how to win in the
first place. =)

| - a player attacks another cross-table because he's got the biggest
| collection of cards and is likely to have the best deck in the table

Penalty on the spot. Players should base decisions on the game state.

| (not because of the raw number but because he has the means whatever
| he wants, including some proven and tested tournament winner
| archetypical decks)

Everyone I know has the potential for a proven, tested
tournament-winner. It's called OBF DOM, and it's made with mostly
commons. The given argument is garbage.

| - a player attacks someone cross-table because he does not like [clan
| X]

Penalty. Players should base decisions on the game state.

| - a player attacks another cross-table because the second has Sudenned
| some master of the first that would get in his way later (say, Ventrue
| Headquarters)

No penalty. The initial Sudden is legal for obvious reasons; so is
in-game retributive action to discourage further Suddens. Everything
here is based on the game state.

| If so, which penalties could be applied? I've been searching for the
| V:EKN penalty guidelines mentioned on the tournament rules and just
| can't find it.

Mostly, just disallow the action, rewind as much as possible (if
necessary), and move on. But few players will call for the judge when
it's happening, so the rewind tends to be beyond the scope of "easily
possible" and the end result is often just "don't do it again".

- --
Derek

Technically, nobody should be able to profit from reputation. Each game
should be its own individual occurrence, with the actions in that game
based entirely on the game state -- and no out-of-game considerations.

Realistically, this is not possible. So while a deal-keeper is
certainly free to refuse any deals made by a deal-breaker, and can
advise other players at the table that this player has broken deals in
the past, he cannot directly act on that information in-game (ie., he
cannot Rush the player to "punish him for breaking deals".)

It's interesting to note from a theoretical standpoint that if
out-of-game information and communication were impossible (the ideal
state of affairs), it is the deal-keeper who suffers rather than the
deal-breaker; the deal-keeper relies on others knowing out-of-game
information that persists between games to either gain his own
"advantage", or to remove a deal-breaker's advantage. The deal-breaker,
on the other hand, gains an advantage; others must trust him at their
own peril, since they know nothing about whether he will keep his word
or not.

This sort of environment would likely lead to almost no long-term deals
being made, and noticeably fewer short-term deals. And it certainly
makes one wonder about the relative strength of a strategy which
_relies_ on out-of-game considerations to be successful, instead of
simply being good at the game itself.

Derek

Lunatic Eruption/Eagle's Sight deck with no retainers.

information.

deck is going to be lots better than mine, so I have to kill him now."

You describe both the situations above from the perspective of
decisions-based-on-game-state. If you're "about to make a VP", then

in-game reasons for you to retaliate, etc.

question publicy if there are other, less-honored motives for
enforcing deals.

old-timers, no matter how many new players get in and how many
old-timers leave. It passes on from "teacher" to "student" almost like
a canonical behaviour. Demolishing perceived reputations of honor in
the hands of old-timers could strike a chord with the new players
before they get too used or too entangled in the present situation.

I guess this is what happens in here, though on a less drastic level.
I often see old-timers getting out of their way to trick newbies into
a bad deal to wipe out other experienced, skilled players out of the
table early.
I imagine there's nothing wrong with that as a chosen strategy - what
strikes me as odd is the fact that if the newbie discovers in time how
bad it was to him to make that deal, he has to choose between losing
horribly or risking social/moral pressure, usually from the
old-timers. In a non-sanitized environment, no one would condemn the
newbie for realizing how bad is the situation for him and consequently
going back to the main objective - play to win, not to help others
win.

bad judging to get someone removed.

the notion is spread during casual play with so much intensity that no
one even *think* about breaking a deal during a tournament. So when
confronted with rhetoric, the answer is almost always "but I know
deals can be broken" - of course they know, they just taught a
different game from the start. It's a case of omission rather than
putting others into direct submission.

Unfortunately, the scenario is worsened by cultural barriers like
language. Most players often rely on more accomplished players because

Exactly.

For me a deal isn't an oath or a handshake or a contract. It is usually
just trying to point out an option to a player that hasn't considered
it. It we both agree that I've pointed out an option that benefits us
both then we act accordingly. The game state is the glue that keeps
our "deal" from being broken.

On the other hand, if we have a deal that is not mutually beneficial
and the only thing holding it together is someone's oath, there may be
a dealbreak.

> If these personal standards are not met, I prefer not to make
> or accept a deal in the first place. But I support the right of
anyone

In a game at GenCon last year, my prey and predator were scheming
together and my prey offered me some insane deal. He basically
threatened me in some way and got me to agree to leave him alone. He
then proceeded to tap out and then I ousted him the next turn. One
remaining player was particularly upset at me for being a
"deal-breaker". The other players joined in and voiced their
displeasure. Funny thing is that right after the game ended, 3 of the
other players (remember that all chided me during the game) said that
they would break a deal too. One guy was right about to break a deal
but was ousted first. Once we escaped the in-game propaganda, it turned
out that only 1 of the players was truly in the "never break a deal"
camp.

deals/agreements and then the issue basically goes away. Deal-keepers
can make good deals and even the deal-breakers won't break them. Bad
deals, however, are risky.

> underrated nowadays - but that's another cup of tea. Not being honest
> can lead to crime. Dealbreaking in this game is not a crime.

Right. Gotta keep the two separate. I wonder what it is about V:TES
that has created such a high tendency for people to confuse in-game
deal-breaking/deal-keeping with "outer world" morality. Do other games
that allow in-game dishonesty have similar problems?

-Robert

Howdy,

I wasn't sure where to attach this, as it seems generally relevant, but
not to any particular branch of this thread.

I am not by nature I'm not a dealbreaker - I tend to be painfully
honest, bad at bluffing and/or reading others' bluffs, and generally to
be too busy just trying to get my deck to work at all to concern myself
with the abstract distraction of deal creation. But I'm
philosophically very sympathetic to dealbreaking, and make no secret of
the fact that I would break a deal if it would win me a game. (So,
really, I've volunteered for the worst of both worlds... Doh!) None
of which matters, as basically no one ever offers me any deals of any
consequence at all.

As a more or less permanent outsider to V:TES (self-taught, no 'mentor'
except you lovable losers, hanging onto whatever playgroup(s) I can
locate in the various places I've lived, and too married-with-kids at
this point to really play very regularly), I guess my perspective on
the topic of dealmaking/breaking is kind of...different?

My experience is that the 'no-dealbreaking' school of thought arises
from the clique structure of many (most?) playgroups. A bunch of
people play together for years (and probably over many different
games): they all know each other and what to expect from each other.
There is no unexpected dealbreaking (unless they're really good players
and/or friends), so there is no real point in dealbreaking. At some
point this gets codified into the social pressure structures of the
group.

Random stranger X joins playgroup. Will they offer him deals? Duh.
No. In almost any case in V:TES, there is at least one other player at
the table that they know better with whom to deal. Even if they can't
get as good a deal from them, well, they at least know what _kind_ of
deal they'll get - plus they probably not only have a good idea of the
clique member's play style, but also probably have played against his
deck before, so they can greatly minimize their risk, if not maximize
their benefit.

Unfortunately this structure is self-reinforcing, as it is difficult to
win at all under these conditions (you against the table), and thus it
is difficult to develop any influence. If stranger X never wins, then,
1) he's clearly the weakest link, so what can he possibly offer, and 2)
boy would it be embarrasing to lose to him, so everyone does whatever
they can to avoid his winning, if it looks at all like a possibility.

(This is less true for 'real' new players, at least to an extent - they
usually get a kind of 'honeymoon' to learn the game _and_ integrate
into the group.)

Anyway, this is getting more tearful and whiny and personal than I
wanted it. Maybe it's just a coincidence that the playgroups I've been
in have been very anti-dealbreaking (though it sounds like Chicago has
moved on from that - Howdy, John 'n' Eric! - interestingly at a point
where the structure for V:TES fell apart and then reintegrated across a
bunch of playgroups...)? I guess I'd be interested to know whether
dealbreaking is generally an advanced or aquired trait of playgroups,
or if some groups have just been that way all along? Is dealbreaking a
conspiracy foisted onto a hapless V:TES playing population by way of an
r.g.t-c.jyhad Usenet meme? If so, can I get some more around here?
Other helpful suggestions for breaking the dealkeeping virus?

Inquiring minds wanna know,
Alex

No suspension, but there is an allowance for a legaly-made deal.

If making the deal with the intention of honoring conformed to
"play to win" at the time it was made, then the rules allow the
deal to be honored (the alternative would effectively elimate
deal-making, as nearly all deals would have to be broken by
application of the play-to-win rules).

Follow-up to the suggestion.

I've just added a new Limited event to happen at my house.
Since we usually play at a store on Saturdays unless when we have
tournaments on the same weekend (usually on Sundays), I'll run a
Limited new type of event on every Friday night before a "real"
tourney. Is is called V:TES Roleplay Day.

It will be handled like a normal tournament, except for these factors:

- "entry fee" is just a common card. of course, anyone can contribute
with any card he wishes, but I don't expect to see more than one or
two odd uncommons in there. These will build up to a prize box to be
used later. I'll include promos in the box when available.

- players are encouraged to, hm, roleplay. Mostly it is restricted to
dialogue and actions against predator or prey, since the Play to Win
rule is still being observed (of course, cross-table play does not
constitute itself in violation, but when acting cross-table the Play
to Win rule is still to be applied. That means a random given
"roleplay-based" decision is still under the Play to Win rule, like
Assamites torporizing cross-table Tremere just because they hate them
on the RPG, and will be penalized if it is not tied to a game-state
situation).

- deal breaking is acceptable. at the worst scenario, I'm the judge
and this is my house, so nobody is allowed to act against
deal-breakers without a good game-state reason. I'm also trying to
stress that deal-breaking in this Limited tournament must not be
considered a reason for players to conclude that player X or Y is
going to break deals on regular casual play or sancioned tournaments.
Hope with time this will make people attent to the deals they make,
and therefore be less concerned about others breaking deals than they
are now.

The winner of the tournament will gain a booster pack and maybe a
special promo. Other players will choose a card from the prize box, in
this order:

- the best "roleplayer" as voted by the participants.
- the most "bastard" deal-breaker, judged by me, according to
accomplishment (GW/VPs/anything gained through breaking the deal) and
roleplaying significance (say, a Ravnos breaking a non-aggression deal
to steal an Assault Rifle and using it to torporize his prey's minions
is better than a Ventrue simply bleeding a tapped out prey for no VP).
Of course this is totally subjective, but is has to be, since it adds
a "fun" factor to deal-breaking. Giving players the chance to vote on
the "best deal-breaking" could result in collusion at this stage. I
expect princes to side with the idea to form some sort of jury next
editions.
- second player
- third player
- fourth player
- fifth player.

If the "best roleplayer" and "most bastard player" are among the top
5, they choose one card for their "roleplaying" accomplishment and a
second one only after all other prized players (so if the "most
bastard" ends up second place, he chooses a card after the "best
roleplayer" and a second one after the fifth place, and so on).

If the idea works, I'm sure something will surface to turn this into a
Build Your Own Storyline series.

I expect players to initially refuse to accept deals, but with time
they will think better and see how the deal-breaking possibility
doesn't preclude nobody from *keeping* deals if they're made in the
best interests of all involved. Once we reach that point, I expect
things to happen outside V:TES Roleplay Day.
